The 90-minute trial uses the fictional adult A, materials M1—M3 and the observation log provided in the entry exercise on this page: first screen materials according to authorisation, then complete the record, the stop and the handover note, and finally compare with the reference answer. Do not contact real clients, do not assess real works and do not claim therapeutic effects.

Work signals for continued exploration: you are willing to observe the creative process around therapeutic goals, record the client's own words separately from your own hypotheses, attend to material safety and privacy, and accept supervision review. Before investing in formal training, first use the complete fictional scenario on this page to practise recording and boundary checking, then verify the education, licence and institutional conditions of the target post; these signals are not a personality type or proof of clinical competence.

Education, certification, licensing, institutional authorisation and signing responsibility are verified separately. In the O*NET new-hire education question, 97% of respondents answered that a master's is required and 3% answered that a post-master's certificate is required; this is respondent opinion, not the education composition of current staff. AATA's education statement lists a master's and supervised internship; ATCB 2026 ATR normally requires first obtaining ATR-P and then meeting post-graduation supervised experience, with reciprocal recognition verified separately. Certification cannot replace a state licence or an employer's clinical authorisation.

In one sentence: this is an occupation that uses art media as the therapeutic vehicle, centres on clinical goals and the therapeutic relationship, and relies on records and teamwork. Competence depends on verifiable performance in supervised practice, not on artistic level or personality labels.

The work of art therapists can be divided into three categories: first, therapeutic tasks using art media and the creative process as the vehicle (assessing needs, designing the course of treatment, conducting guided self-expression, observing and recording responses); second, preparation and safety work directly related to the creative setting (selecting and preparing media and equipment, assessing material risk, and storing works and records according to the rules); third, tasks involving collaboration with the treatment team and the institution (reviewing with physicians, nurses, psychological professionals, rehabilitation staff and supervisors, writing treatment plans and case summaries, supervising interns and referring on according to procedure). The three categories share one goal: to make the intervention clear in purpose, appropriate in media, safe in process and traceable in records.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET-SOC 29-1129.01 Art Therapists, Bright Outlook, updated in 2026; the official duty is to plan or conduct art therapy sessions or programmes to improve clients' physical, cognitive or emotional health. The page lists 27 tasks, including conducting guided self-expression, building a relationship with the client and reviewing their responses, assessing client needs, designing session goals, selecting and preparing art media, observing and recording progress, collaborating with the treatment team, writing treatment plans and case summaries, supervising interns, and initiating crisis intervention and referral in client emergencies. The current 27 tasks comprise 22 core, 3 supplementary and 2 unscored new tasks (safely storing works, and in a crisis contacting emergency personnel to coordinate treatment); an unscored task is not taken to mean it is unimportant, and no authority to act is self-granted.

Goals and media｜Choosing media according to therapeutic goals, sensory and motor ability, material risk and cultural background, and stating the boundaries of this session's activity｜An activity plan in which goals, media and activity boundaries correspond one-to-one.

Process and observation｜Conducting guided self-expression, observing the creative process and verbal responses, and discussing the experience with the client without mechanically interpreting symbols in the work as diagnosis｜A process record containing specific observational evidence and the client's own words.

Recording and review｜Recording therapeutic goals, activities and progress, and reviewing with the team according to the approved division of labour｜An editorial example record; it is not guaranteed that all judgements can be fully traced.

Collaboration and escalation｜O*NET includes teamwork, supervision and, in an emergency, contacting emergency personnel to coordinate treatment; your specific authority and the stop and referral procedures are verified against the actual rules｜An editorial handover note; this page does not prescribe a uniform on-site operating procedure.

Boundaries and responsibility｜Section 4 of the AATA treats works as the client's property and as protected information, and in some settings they can become clinical records; copying, display, custody and retention periods are verified against the relevant consent and rules｜It is not generalised that every work is a service record, and the destruction authority was not fully verified this round.

Communication and contact｜86% of respondents have face-to-face discussions every day, 66% report continuous contact with others, 77% use email every day and 43% use the telephone every day (O*NET work context respondent proportions, Art Therapists (O*NET-SOC 29-1129.01) detailed occupation).
Decision latitude and freedom｜71% have a great deal of decision freedom, 66% have a great deal of freedom to determine tasks, priorities and goals, and 63% make decisions every day.
Team and influence｜49% consider teamwork extremely important, 38% consider their decisions to have an important effect on colleagues or institutional results, and 29% consider they bear very high responsibility for the health and safety of others.
Environment and body｜89% work indoors in a controlled environment every day, 57% sit more than half the time, 54% have physical proximity within arm's length of others, and 40% continually use their hands to handle objects and tools.
Pressure and conflict｜43% face time pressure once a week or more but not every day, 51% deal with conflict situations once a week or more but not every day, and 37% deal with unpleasant, angry or discourteous people once a week or more but not every day.
Objects and settings｜Service users cover children, adolescents, adults and older people, in settings such as schools, care facilities, health centres, prisons, shelters and hospitals.

Materials and records｜The work involves referral information, art materials such as drawing and clay, client works, process observations and treatment records; custody, photography and destruction of works must follow institutional rules and privacy requirements.
Qualification and training｜O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone Five (SVP 8.0 and above); 97% of respondents consider a master's degree necessary and 3% consider a post-master's certificate necessary; ATCB's ATR-P is usually the prerequisite credential for ATR, and ATR additionally requires post-graduation supervised experience (reciprocal recognition paths verified separately).

Art therapists use art media and the creative process as the core vehicle of therapeutic work; clinical and counselling psychologists cover broader psychological assessment and psychological services, marriage and family therapists use the relational system as the unit of analysis, mental health counsellors focus on talking and counselling plans, and rehabilitation counsellors focus on disability adjustment and employment and life goals. Adjacent occupations may use creative methods, but they do not thereby become art therapy.
Achieving therapeutic goals through the art process
Under clear therapeutic goals, using visual art media and the creative process to support the client's physical, cognitive or emotional wellbeing.
Referral information, works and process observation
Based on the purpose of the referral, existing records, the client's consent and institutional authorisation; the objects include media such as drawing and clay, client works and process observation.

Art therapists (US O*NET-SOC 29-1129.01) plan or conduct art therapy with goals involving physical, cognitive or emotional wellbeing; the work includes assessing needs, selecting media, recording the process and working with the team. Teaching and therapy have different goals and responsibilities, and a drawing activity cannot by itself imply a therapeutic qualification. In mainland China, the diagnosis of mental disorders is made by licensed psychiatrists; assessment and diagnostic authority in other jurisdictions must be verified against your own licence and cannot be judged from the occupational title alone.
Assess—design—create—record
Assessing needs, setting goals, selecting media, conducting guided self-expression, observing responses, recording progress and adjusting subsequent goals.
Traceable treatment records
Treatment records and work custody notes in which goals are clear, media are appropriate, the process is safe and records are traceable and can support subsequent care decisions.
Those trained and authorised

On-site judgement and recording are the responsibility of art therapists with the corresponding training and institutional authorisation; where beyond scope, a supervisor or the corresponding professional bears it.
Training, licensing and institutional authorisation

Your training scope, state licensing and title rules, the institutional authorisation chain and supervision arrangements together determine what you may do, and these cannot be created by a short course or an overseas certificate.
Not interchangeable

The adjacent occupations have different directions: if you prefer teaching outcomes, structured psychological assessment, relational system work or employment rehabilitation, compare the training and authorisation of the corresponding occupations separately.

At least six items must be verified before starting: the occupational measure and the post entity, education and the supervised pathway, licensing and title rules, institutional authorisation and supervision arrangements, record and privacy responsibility, and the real pay structure and working hours.
Occupational measure

On the US side it is O*NET-SOC 29-1129.01; in mainland China first identify whether the post belongs to art education, rehabilitation activities, psychosocial services or psychological treatment within a medical institution, as the four have different authorisation.
Education and the supervised pathway

US professional education: AATA lists master's-level education with at least 100 hours of supervised practicum and 600 hours of clinical internship. ATCB 2026 ATR normally has ATR-P as a prerequisite; for those meeting the designated programme pathway there are 1,000 hours of post-graduation direct contact and 100 hours of supervision (of which 50 hours ATR-BC), with bridging or reciprocal recognition paths verified separately. In-programme internship and post-graduation experience cannot be added together.
Licensing and titles

ATR/ATR-BC are ATCB professional certifications; ATCB makes clear that it does not issue or regulate state licences. The lawful scope of service, title protection and independent practice conditions in the target state must be verified with that state's authorities, and employer authorisation does not replace a licence required by law.
Institutional authorisation and supervision

Confirm the nature of the institution, the approved scope of service, the supervision arrangements and the escalation chain; in mainland China, the diagnosis of mental disorders is made by licensed psychiatrists and psychotherapy should be carried out within medical institutions.
Records and privacy

Works, photographs, session records and cloud prompts may contain sensitive information; check the consent, storage, display, cross-border and destruction rules, and removing names does not always equal completed de-identification.
Pay and working hours

Posts with the same title may use a monthly salary, a per-teaching-period fee or a project fee; when comparing, include guaranteed hours, preparation and record-keeping time, supervision costs, social insurance and the cancellation policy in the written contract.

Art therapists form the intervention and the clinical record through visual art media, the creative process and the therapeutic relationship; music therapists use musical experience as the core medium, occupational therapists work around daily activity function and rehabilitation goals, and low vision and orientation and mobility rehabilitation posts focus on visual function compensation, environmental navigation and independent living training. Choosing a direction should compare the main output, the service users and the authorisation, not reputation.

This table compares only directions belonging to different occupational classifications; the degree, supervised practice and licensing requirements of adjacent occupations must be verified separately by jurisdiction, and this page does not present any direction as a shortcut to a career change.

Music therapy uses musical experience (singing, playing, rhythm and improvisation) as the core medium, and assessment and recording revolve around musical behaviour; the therapeutic goal structure of the two is similar, but the media system, material safety and professional continuing education content differ.

If you find it easier to build a relationship and observe change through visual materials and image expression, examine art therapy first; if musical experience is your core form of expression, you should compare music therapy.
Using visual art media and the creative process as the therapeutic vehicle, with outputs mainly treatment records, work custody notes and interprofessional collaboration conclusions.
Art therapy and music therapy

Occupational therapists focus on life activities, function and environmental adaptation; art therapy uses the art process as its main medium, and both may involve emotional, cognitive and functional goals. The difference lies in the main working method and assessment training, not in art therapy never addressing function.

If your focus is improving specific life activities and functional performance, compare occupational therapy first; if your focus is using the art process to support emotional and cognitive expression, examine art therapy first.
Designing interventions around daily activity function and rehabilitation goals, with outputs mainly functional assessment, activity adaptation plans and life participation goals.
Art therapy and occupational therapy

In mainland China, the diagnosis of mental disorders is made by licensed psychiatrists and psychotherapeutic activity should be carried out within medical institutions; art therapists do not gain diagnostic or prescribing authority by using art media. In other jurisdictions, diagnostic and psychotherapeutic authority is likewise determined by licence and institutional authorisation.

If you want to take on diagnosis and systematic psychotherapy responsibility, you need the corresponding medical or psychology education and licensing path; if you want to use art media as the vehicle of intervention, art therapy should be verified as an independent direction with its own training and authorisation.

Each psychological service direction carries out assessment and treatment within its own training and licensing scope. In mainland China the diagnosis of mental disorders is made by licensed psychiatrists; those specialising in psychotherapy must not diagnose, prescribe or provide surgical treatment, and the authority of different personnel cannot be merged.
Art therapy and the psychotherapy sequence

The main unit of analysis in rehabilitation counselling is disability and vocational function, and the service chain is closer to employment and social security; both may use creative methods, but that does not make rehabilitation counselling into art therapy.

If you are more concerned with employment, disability adjustment and social reintegration, compare rehabilitation counselling first; if you are more concerned with the therapeutic relationship and the creative process itself, examine art therapy first.
Rehabilitation counselling focuses on disability adjustment, employment and life goals, with outputs mainly rehabilitation plans, employment support and case management records.
Art therapy and rehabilitation counselling

Vision rehabilitation occupations centre on visual function, orientation and mobility and independent living skills; art therapy centres on art media and the creative process. The two may share activities or adaptive technology, but professional assessment and qualifications cannot be swapped.

If you want to do functional compensation and independent living training, choose the low vision and vision rehabilitation direction; if you want the creative process to carry therapeutic goals, choose art therapy.
Focusing on visual function compensation, environmental navigation and independent living training, with outputs mainly functional training plans and assistive technology adaptation.
Art therapy and low vision / orientation and mobility rehabilitation

When moving from art education or hobby activities into art therapy, the gap is usually not drawing skill but therapeutic theory, ethics, assessment boundaries, supervised practice and record responsibility; short art activity courses do not constitute clinical training.

If you value teaching outcomes and finished work more, compare the art education direction first; if you are willing to take responsibility for therapeutic goals, records and supervision, then consider art therapy and verify its education and supervised requirements.
Art education produces technique and aesthetic outcomes and general interest activities aim at the participatory experience; neither centres on therapeutic goals and record responsibility.
Moving from art education and general interest activities

Conclusion: the basis for choosing a direction is the main output, the service users and the authorisation chain, not how similar the occupational titles sound; once the direction is decided, verify the education, supervised practice, licensing and institutional authorisation requirements of the target direction item by item.

items.title: What education, certification and ability conditions should be checked to enter the field?

values: Scenario: a 90-minute desktop simulation designed by the FermatMind editorial team, with all people, materials and logs fictional. The learner plays a supervised intern and only does preparation, factual recording and handover, and does not treat real people, assess works or make diagnoses.

Fictional referral: adult A, whose code name contains no personal information. Supervisor D has set the goal of this session as letting A independently choose a paper medium and express the experience of the activity; the trainee may only carry out the preparation and recording confirmed by D and may not add therapeutic goals of their own.

Authorisation and environment: A has consented only to internal process recording and has not consented to photography, teaching display or external cloud processing; A may stop at any time. D can take over immediately at the simulated activity site. Unknown medical history, allergies or material conditions must first be asked of D and cannot be invented.

Material input: M1 paper and a thick-barrelled pencil, which D has confirmed as suitable; M2 scented markers, with allergy information unknown; M3 clay and small accessories, which D has not approved for use. The desktop simulation selects only M1 and does not actually arrange for A to create.

Log input: at 09:00 A chooses M1; at 09:05 A says I want to draw lines first; at 09:10 A stops writing and says I want to stop now, I do not want photographs taken; at 09:11 D takes over and asks that only the exact words and the time be recorded. The log gives no harmful behaviour or diagnosis and none may be added.

60-minute production: list the approved / to-check status and the reason for each material; fill in a five-column record of time, observable event, exact words, action and handover recipient, and state clearly the stop and the privacy handling after 09:10.

Reference answer: M1 is approved, M2 is awaiting D to verify allergy information, and M3 is not approved; do not choose M2/M3 on your own just because a substitute medium is needed. At 09:00 record that A chooses M1; at 09:05 record the exact words verbatim; at 09:10 stop the current arrangement and respect the refusal of photography; at 09:11 hand over to D.

Reference record: 09:10｜stops writing｜I want to stop now, I do not want photographs taken｜stop and do not photograph｜D; 09:11｜D takes over｜record only the exact words and the time｜complete the internal record and mark it for D to review｜D. The wish to stop must not be written as treatment failure, an emotional disorder or a risk level.

30-minute review: mark out separately the log facts, the unresolved material questions and the authority boundaries, and revise against the reference answer. Deliver the material screening table, the four time records and a handover note, all marked fictional exercise.

Counterfactual one: if the scenario adds A's consent to photography but the institution still has not approved external transfer, the photographs must not be uploaded to an external tool; the consent scope and the institutional processing authority must both be satisfied.
Counterfactual two: if the scenario changes so that M1 is also not approved, the answer becomes to arrange no medium for the time being and ask D to verify; the M1 plan cannot be carried over.

Acceptance: the material status matches the scenario; the times and exact words are traceable; after 09:10 the activity is stopped and no photograph is taken; the handover recipient is D; no medical history, diagnosis or treatment effect is added. If one item is missing, revise first and then complete the exercise.

These scoring items are editorial exercise rules that test reading, recording and authority checking; they are not clinical competence certification, treatment effect evaluation or formal supervision. Real emergencies must be handled according to the institution's and the applicable law's emergency procedure, and this simulation does not train emergency medical handling.
